In the Oyster toadfish (Opsanus tau), the transition from pelagic egg to free-living larva is a critical developmental bottleneck. Eggs are demersal and adhesive, deposited in sheltered cavities by nest-guarding males. Incubation proceeds relatively slowly compared to many subtropical teleosts; at a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the period from fertilisation to eclosion lasts approximately 30 days . The newly emerged prolarva is endotrophic, subsisting entirely on its yolk reserve during the first days post-hatch. At the moment of chorion rupture, the total length of the yolk-sac larva is typically around 1.55 cm [Lb = around 1.55 cm], a modest size that reflects the substantial yolk investment required to sustain the non-feeding interval until mouth opening and retinal differentiation permit first exogenous feeding. This lecithotrophic phase is energetically demanding, and survival through the yolk absorption stage is strongly temperature-dependent. Once the trophic switch to active feeding occurs, the young individual enters a rapid juvenile growth phase, during which the developing fish must reach a sufficient size to avoid gape-limited predators common in estuarine nursery habitats along the eastern coast of North America.

Juvenile Oyster toadfish exhibit a protracted period of somatic development before the onset of gonadal maturation. Under the thermal regime typical of their northern range, sustained at approximately 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C], the first successful spawning event is not observed until roughly 1,058 days after hatching [tR = roughly 1,058 days after hatching]. This age at first reproduction, equivalent to just under three years, aligns well with the field-based estimate of two to three years reported by MensStep2001 for this species in Mid-Atlantic Bight populations. The delay reflects a life-history strategy in which the individual prioritises the accumulation of body mass and energy reserves before investing in reproductive effort. Before this milestone, the juvenile and sub-adult fish undergo steady increases in both length and wet weight. Growth trajectories are asymptotic, with the ultimate total length that a fully grown adult can attain estimated at 43.2 cm [Li = 43.2 cm], a size that places Opsanus tau among the larger members of the Batrachoididae. Comparable data from the congeneric Lusitanian toadfish Halobatrachus didactylus indicate that total length at puberty in that species is approximately 25 cm [Lp = approximately 25 cm], suggesting a broadly similar allometric scaling of maturation size within the family.

As the Oyster toadfish approaches its asymptotic body size, the rate of length increment declines considerably while mass continues to accrue. The maximum recorded wet weight in adults, or ultimate wet weight, has been documented at 2,200 grams [Wwi = 2,200 grams] for large, gravid females collected from Chesapeake Bay populations. This substantial mass is accompanied by a robust, benthic body plan well suited to life among oyster reefs and rocky substrates where the species ambushes crustacean and fish prey. Reproductive output scales positively with female size, and the relationship between maternal length and fecundity has been characterised for this species. At a standard length of 34.5 cm, females exhibit a reproductive rate of approximately 3.3 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 3.3 offspring per day]  when maintained at a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This daily reproductive rate reflects the production of adhesive eggs deposited in a single clutch guarded by the male. Given the protracted spawning season, which can extend from late spring through early autumn in the northern portion of the range, total annual fecundity can be substantial, though it is partitioned into discrete nesting events.

Longevity estimates for Opsanus tau suggest a notably long lifespan relative to many other estuarine teleosts of comparable body size. Field recapture data and otolith-based ageing studies indicate that the maximum recorded lifespan under natural conditions reaches approximately 7,300 days [am = approximately 7,300 days], a value equivalent to at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]about 20 years. This remarkable longevity is likely facilitated by the species' low metabolic demands during the winter months when activity is suppressed, combined with a robust nesting strategy that reduces adult predation risk. This extended lifespan is supported by measurements taken at a seasonal average temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], which is representative of the cooler bottom waters the fish experiences during winter dormancy. For comparison, many confamilial species from tropical waters exhibit substantially shorter life expectancies, often less than half this duration, a pattern consistent with the well-known latitudinal gradient in ectotherm longevity. The slow life history of Opsanus tau, characterised by delayed maturation and low adult mortality, is typical of a benthic sit-and-wait predator operating in a relatively stable, low-energy environment.

The nesting biology of the Oyster toadfish exerts a strong influence on its life history schedule. Males establish territories under rocks or within abandoned burrows and emit a characteristic boatwhistle advertisement call to attract gravid females. Following gamete release and external fertilisation within the nest, the male assumes exclusive parental care, fanning the demersal egg mass and aggressively defending it against intruders for the entire incubation period. The total length at which males first become capable of successful nest guarding and courtship, effectively the size at functional puberty, is estimated to be 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm] based on comparisons with the closely related Lusitanian toadfish Halobatrachus didactylus. This size threshold correlates with the development of the sonic swim bladder musculature necessary for producing the advertisement call.
